text.p: These are the highlights of the main Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro newspapers this morning.
-- SURVEY SHOWS POPULATION IS OPTIMISTIC ABOUT 1997

Brasilians appear to be optimistic about the coming year. According to a Gallup-Gazeta Mercantil poll, 66 percent of the population believes 1997 will be a better year than the last and 16 percent believe it will at least as good as 1996.

Driven by the debate surrounding the re-election amendment, Brazil's congress could bring a far-ranging political reform project to the negotiating table. Both in the Senate and in the Lower House two projects, including electoral reform changes, have been placed on the voting schedule.
-- NEW MAYOR WILL BUILD HALF-WAY HOUSES FOR BEGGARS

Rio de Janeiro's mayor-elect Luiz Paulo Conde, said cariocas will have to learn to live with beggars on the street as this is a problem that several major cities around the world. He said he would seek alternative solutions to the problem including the construction of half-way houses where people will be given a bed and food to eat.

Rio police arrested a group of 12 thieves suspected of committing up to 230 holdups over the last five months. The group, 15 of which are still free, would mug drivers at traffic-lights using guns loaned by drug-traffickers.
-- CHILDREN OF THE LANDLESS PEASANT MOVEMENT DROP OUT

The sons and daughters of Brazil's landless peasant movement (MST) are leaving the rural encampments to study in the nearby towns and cities. A MST survey showed only 11 percent of the people living in the encampments are between the ages of 13 and 18. Forty-one percent are adults.
